title: 10 Best-Selling EVs in the US in the First Half of 2026
content:
Automotive & Mobility
Market Analysis
US EV sales fell 23.8% after the federal tax credit expired, yet these 10 models still accounted for 72% of all EVs sold.
August 17, 2026
10 Slides
Start slideshow
Tesla Model Y.
For most of the past decade, electric vehicle sales in the US grew every single year. Federal tax credits and state rebates fueled this consistent growth, leading automakers to build battery plants all across the country, like in Georgia, Tennessee, and Michigan. Everyone in the auto industry seemed to believe the $7,500 federal clean vehicle tax credit was a permanent fixture of the market.
That is, until Congress ended the tax credit on September 30, 2025. Buyers rushed to make their purchases in the third quarter of 2025 to beat the deadline, but the market still shrank as expected. For the first half of 2026,
Kelley Blue Book estimates
US EV sales fell to roughly 463,000 units, down 23.8% from the same period a year earlier. Sales in the second quarter alone fell 20.5% year over year.
Automakers responded by cutting prices instead of production. Several brands took $7,500 to $9,800 off their entire electric lineups in the months after the deadline, absorbing the lost credit themselves to keep sticker prices palatable for consumers. Others introduced cheaper entry trims with smaller battery packs, trading range for a sub-$40,000 MSRP.

We've put together a list of the 10 best-selling EVs in the US for the first half of this year. Read on to learn about what propelled each model to the top.

title: US drone battery makers target China supply
content:
Automotive & Mobility
Battery Manufacturing
Amprius Technologies and Packet Digital are scaling domestic drone battery production to reduce Pentagon reliance on Chinese suppliers for UAS programs.
August 17, 2026
5 Min Read
A member of the US Army 7th Army Training Command pilots an ADM4 surveillance drone.
Sean Gallup/Getty Images
At a Glance
Amprius ships 450 Wh/kg silicon-anode cells from California pilot line to multiple drone customers
Packet Digital receives $9.8 million Navy contract to scale lithium-ion cell production in Fargo
Pentagon's Blue UAS fleet still uses Chinese batteries despite 2020 NDAA procurement restrictions
Over the last decade, the U.S. military has grown increasingly dependent on small unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) for many operations. In a UAS, the battery is one of the most important components, determining crucial factors like the aircraft’s endurance, payload, and range. Only a few suppliers worldwide make cells sufficiently performant for UAS, and most of them are based in China.
To bolster national security, the U.S. government sought to limit China’s dominance in UAS battery supply through procurement regulations. In 2020, lawmakers passed the
National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA)
to bar the Department of Defense from buying unmanned aircraft with Chinese flight controllers, radios, or cameras. Unfortunately, the NDAA did not cover components that neither store nor transmit data, such as motors, speed controllers, and batteries. This loophole, combined with China’s supply chain strength, contributed to
the Pentagon’s Blue UAS fleet still using Chinese batteries
Related:
Korean EVs Crush Tesla, German Rivals in Battery Longevity Test
Where regulators see limitations, domestic suppliers see opportunities to help solve this supply chain crisis. In this piece, we'll take a look at two battery suppliers in the U.S. that are ramping up production for the military’s drone program,
Amprius Technologies
Packet Digital
Drone batteries’ production challenges
Drones need batteries that are both lightweight and high-power to balance performance, range, and efficiency. Therefore, the ideal drone battery is the one that offers the most energy per unit weight.
In many cases, the primary constraint on a battery cell’s energy density is its anode material. While graphite is the industry-standard anode material for Li-ion batteries,
it has an energy density of only 372 mAh/g.
In contrast, silicon has an energy density of 3,579 mAh/g, meaning a silicon-based battery could theoretically offer 10x greater energy per unit weight.
The catch, however, is that silicon can swell up to 300% as it charges in a lithium-ion battery, which cracks particles and shortens cell life. To mitigate these risks, battery manufacturers can nanostructure the silicon and build void space into the particles, but that is difficult and costly to do at commercial scale.
Benefits of nanostructured silicon for lithium-ion battery anodes. Credit: Pavlovskii et al.
Anode chemistry is only half the reason many drone battery suppliers are located offshore. The other half is the fact that U.S. battery manufacturers don’t produce enough drone batteries to meet military demand. Instead, Chinese suppliers eclipse domestic ones in both volume and cost.
To onshore drone battery production, domestic manufacturers must either build batteries with much higher energy density or standard cells at higher volumes.
Related:
10 Best-Selling EVs in the US in the First Half of 2026
Amprius’ Fremont pilot line
Amprius Technologies is one of the first domestic suppliers to produce high-energy-density silicon batteries. In July 2025, the company
announced
that it had delivered its silicon-anode battery cells to multiple drone and UAS customers from its Fremont, California, pilot line.
According to the company, those shipments included 450 Wh/kg high-energy cells to AALTO, an Airbus subsidiary, along with balanced energy-and-power cells for tactical and commercial drone makers. Amprius says third-party testing has validated its batteries at 500 Wh/kg and 1,300 Wh/L.
Amprius ships high-performance silicon anode cells to multiple drone customers from its US pilot line. Credit: Amprius Technologies.
This level of energy density is significant for endurance UAS. For example, AALTO’s Zephyr is a solar-powered solution, meaning it needs to store enough energy during the day to fly through the night. According to Pierre-Antoine Aubourg, chief technology officer at AALTO, “[Amprius’] silicon anode technology has already enabled Zephyr to operate in the stratosphere overnight for months at a time.”
Despite all this promising news, Amprius can’t replace Chinese battery suppliers because it still can’t produce at scale. At the moment, Amprius’ Fremont facility is primarily an R&D hub, with the company planning to contract out cell manufacturing abroad. So far, the company claims to have already secured more than 1.8 GWh of production capacity, including an agreement in South Korea. Therefore, the Pentagon will have to wait if it wants fully domestically-made batteries for its entire UAS program.
Related:
GM Exits Samsung SDI Battery Venture as Ohio Ultium Plant Restarts Production
Packet Digital’s Navy cell plant
Whereas Amprius was targeting high energy density, Packet Digital is targeting high capacity cell production.
In May, Packet Digital and its subsidiary Badland Batteries
announced
that the U.S. Navy had awarded them $9.8 million to enter Phase 3 of their contract under the Logistics UAS Family of Advanced Batteries program. Badland previously started commissioning its Fargo, North Dakota factory, so Phase 3 will cover production scaling and supply chain validation as it ramps up throughput to meet Navy requirements.
In addition to building out manufacturing capacity for NDAA-compliant cells, Badland says it will use the Phase 3 funds to support multiple lithium-ion chemistries to meet changing Navy requirements. According to Terri Zimmerman, CEO of Packet Digital, “Phase 3 is where years of planning, engineering and investment turn into high-rate production capability for the U.S. Navy, national defense and commercial markets.”
The U.S. Navy contract also brings political benefits. U.S. Sen. John Hoeven said the funding “keeps that work moving forward in North Dakota, supports good-paying manufacturing jobs and helps ensure a secure supply chain while reducing our reliance on materials from adversaries.” Because Phase 3 has just begun, it’s worth noting that no one knows whether Badland will successfully produce UAS cells at volumes high enough to replace Chinese manufacturers.
Two routes to the same capability
The announcements showcase two companies contributing to a domestic drone battery supply chain. Amprius sits at one end, aiming for energy densities that outcompete imported cells, and Packet Digital sits at the other, building manufacturing capacity that rivals offshore suppliers.
While there is hope for domestic cell production, throughput has yet to be proven. With the NDAA and other laws still permitting the U.S. military to import batteries from China, the future of domestic drone batteries may hinge on whether they can be competitive on a cost-per-watt-hour basis.

title: Stord: How a $3bn Logistics Platform is Driving Commerce
content:
Stord: How a $3bn Logistics Platform is Driving Commerce
Prioritise Us
on Google
Stord is expanding its capabilities with launch of Stord Labs and recent funding round | Sean Henry, CEO and Co-Founder of Stord (L) and Jacob Boudreau, CTO and Co-Founder of Stord (R). Credit: Sean Henry
Following a US$3bn valuation and a US$250m round of funding, Stord is using its logistics expertise to help close the AI gap for retail giants
In an era of ongoing complexity, advanced solutions are necessary for driving resilience across every industry.
Having grown significantly, Stord is
advancing robotics
and next-generation AI across commerce, helping transform the retail landscape.
This year, the company received a major sum in its Series F funding, leading to a US$3bn valuation. Now, its expanded capabilities and launch of Stord Labs is helping it deliver superior consumer experiences.
Commerce optimisation tools
Organisations around the world are looking to transform their operations, particularly as global supply chains become more complex. Commerce supply chains are facing significant complexity, as trade routes are being rewritten due to volatility and relationship changes, and demand is at an all-time high.
The rise of ecommerce over the past few years has grown the need for fast and reliable logistics, which means that many companies have turned to optimisation platforms and other digital tools.
Stord acts as a physical intelligence layer for independent commerce, offering software, AI and robotics support, as well as access to a resilient and efficient fulfilment network. This helps brands take greater control of their supply chain, with increased visibility and capabilities across every part of the commerce journey,
including returns
Stord, founded in 2015, aims to help brands grow their revenue capabilities, reduce costs and meet consumer expectations. It offers independent commerce brands with the same capabilities that larger organisations have, helping them grow their operations with more mainstream opportunities.
Currently, Stord helps more than 1,000 brands, with a network spanning approximately 100 fulfilment locations around the world. In May 2026, the company received a nearly US$250m Series F funding round at a US$3bn valuation. The round was led by Strike Capital, Kleiner Perkins, Founders Fund, Franklin Templeton, Baillie Gifford,  G Squared, Bond and Lux.
"For years, every independent brand has been left to figure out on their own how to compete against the consumer experience Amazon has spent decades and hundreds of billions building," explains Sean Henry, Founder and CEO of Stord.
Sean Henry, CEO of Stord
"By every measure, independent brands have been losing. Stord exists to level that playing field. We give independent brands the complete commerce stack: the fulfillment network, software and AI, to deliver a consumer experience that surpasses Prime.
"Our vertical integration and scaled network create compounding advantages that deliver better, faster, cheaper outcomes with every order we touch. As AI and physical intelligence advance across our platform, that advantage for our customers is rapidly accelerating.”
The funding
helps Stord to provide more independent brands with increased capabilities to own their direct consumer relationships, offering them greater agency with their operations.
AI and automation
Alongside the funding news, Stord also announced the launch of Stord Labs, a physical intelligence lab at its Atlanta headquarters. Here, the company is developing and
trialing agentic AI
, robotics and advanced automation. It is exploring how these tools operate on real orders in the production network in order to see if they actively improve workflow.
Stord Labs relies on automation to drive efficiency. Credit: Stord
Stord is training models on live fulfilment data, making use of eight billion data points every year. Through this, the network is becoming smarter, faster and more cost effective.
The aim of the company is to meet the capabilities of ecommerce and logistics giants, like Amazon, but to hold on to the feeling of independent commerce. This is helping drive diversity and choice within commerce – as more consumers want faster delivery with trackable data, organisations which fail to offer these solutions risk loosing out on customers.
Through Stord's work of aiding independent brands with these solutions, it is helping independent brands meet demand and stay in the commerce competition. This, in turn, offers consumers more choice as to who they shop with.
In its past four years of operations, Stord's revenue has grown more than 10x. As a result, it powers more than US$15bn in GMV every year and its packages reach almost one in four US households. Its rapid growth comes alongside the growth in commerce – especially as consumers are beginning to consciously think more about their purchasing.
Consumers are prioritising independent brands, or those that demonstrate a conscious sustainability initiative. However, some are turned away by the lessened capabilities these provide. Stord, therefore, is working to bridge this gap, and, with its newest
round of funding
and the introduction of Stord Labs, it can.

title: What Does the US-Saudi Nuclear Deal Mean for Operations?
content:
What Does the US-Saudi Nuclear Deal Mean for Operations?
Prioritise Us
on Google
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and US President Donald Trump. Credit: The White House
The US and Saudi Arabia have signed a nuclear cooperation deal, which will boost efficiency and availability, but some leaders show concerns of tensions
A nuclear cooperation agreement between the US and
Saudi Arabia
signed on 22 July could reshape equipment supply chains and create new procurement pathways for American manufacturers over the next three decades.
The pact, which pairs a peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement with a bilateral safeguards arrangement, was signed by US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright and Saudi Minister of Energy Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman al-Saud.
The deal is expected to run for around 30 years and could be worth tens of billions of US dollars to American firms. Westinghouse Electric Company has been named as a likely partner, with its CEO Dan Sumner calling the agreement a step that "strengthens
energy security
" and expands opportunities for US industry.
Dan Sumner, CEO of Westinghouse. Credit: Westinghouse
Domestic enrichment and fuel supply
The agreement could alter uranium
fuel supply chains
in ways that differ from established nuclear trade patterns. Reports suggest the new deal could eventually allow
Saudi Arabia
to enrich uranium domestically at a US-built facility, subject to a two-year joint study, rather than importing finished fuel as most nuclear energy nations choose to do.
Civilian power plants typically need uranium enriched to around 3.67%. Weapons-grade material requires enrichment above 90%.
Rosemary Kelanic, Director of the Middle East programme at the Defense Priorities think tank, calls the prospect "quite shocking", noting that Washington has never previously helped a partner nation enrich uranium on its own soil. The enrichment question is the detail that has energy analysts and non-proliferation experts most concerned.
Rosemary Kelanic, Director of the Middle East programme at Defense Priorities. Credit: Defense Priorities
Chris described the arrangement as one that upholds the "highest standards of nuclear safety and non-proliferation".
Comparing oversight and procurement models
Industry watchers have been quick to measure this agreement against the 2009 US-United Arab Emirates (UAE) nuclear deal. Washington has previously called this agreement the "gold standard" for such deals because Abu Dhabi agreed never to enrich or reprocess nuclear fuel.
The UAE also accepted the International Atomic Energy Agency's Additional Protocol, a stricter inspection regime used to verify peaceful use. The Saudi agreement is reported to fall short of that standard, with Riyadh not expected to accept the same level of IAEA oversight.
The difference in oversight regimes could mean different equipment specifications and compliance requirements for US suppliers. According to The Guardian, the agreement must now go to Congress, where opposition has been vocal but is unlikely to be decisive.
Congressional review and industry reaction
Democratic Congressman John Garamendi calls it a "consequential mistake", while Senator Chris Murphy warns it could "set off a nuclear race in the region". Republican reaction has been more muted, with Representative Marlin Stutzman saying he has no "initial" concerns.
Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State, has dismissed concerns over the US's new nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia. Credit: Wikimedia Commons
Blocking the deal would require a joint resolution passed by a two-thirds majority in both chambers, a threshold critics are widely expected to fall short of. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, one of
President Trump
's right-hand men, has dismissed proliferation concerns.
Marco has said that the US is "not going to reach any agreement with any country in the world that leads to the risk of proliferation". The deal comes at a strange time for US foreign policy, and for geopolitics more broadly.
The US's conflict with Iran is still rumbling on, while the US-Russia arms control treaty, known as New START, officially expired in February this year. As a result, international tensions regarding nuclear proliferation are higher than they have been in several years.

title: BYD's cheapest EV spotted with an upgraded interior and a single large display screen
content:
Peter Johnson
| Aug 17 2026 - 8:38 am PT
low-cost Seagull EV, sold as the Dolphin Surf in Europe and Dolphin Mini in other overseas markets, is due for an upgrade. Here’s a sneak peek.
BYD prepares to launch the new Seagull EV
The current 2026 Seagull starts at just 69,900 yuan in China, or about $10,000, making it BYD’s most affordable pure electric vehicle.
It’s also among BYD’s most popular models. According to data compiled by
Cleantechnica
, BYD’s Seagull (Dolphin Mini/Dolphin Surf) was the sixth-best-selling EV globally through the first half of 2026.
With new competition emerging, BYD is preparing to introduce the upgraded Seagull. The new version is expected to roll out in China first, then to overseas markets.
About a month ago, Zhang Zhuo, the sales boss of BYD’s Ocean series,
previewed the new Seagull
for the first time, posting several blurry images on social media.
The caption read, “As its silhouette gradually emerges in the shadows, the promise of growing up is about to be fulfilled. #BYDSseagull#.”
While it’s still blurry, you can see the new version has a LiDAR on the roof to support new ADAS features.
While BYD has yet to announce the details, the new Seagull was released in the batch of new energy vehicles approved for sale by China’s
Ministry of Industry and Information Technology
(MIIT) last month, revealing a few new upgrades.
For one, the new Seagull is a bit longer than the current version. According to the release, the upgraded Seagull measures 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm tall, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase. In comparison, the current Seagull is just 3,780 mm long.
While the interior was expected to feature BYD’s updated design, a new spy photo from
ThinkerCar
offers a sneak peek.
An alleged spy shot of the all-new
Seagull interior has surfaced. The model is reportedly set for comprehensive upgrades to styling, cabin, dimensions, and powertrain, boosting its competitiveness.
https://t.co/gq4z2Fs9Kd
The upgraded version will also gain a more powerful 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from the 55 kW (75 hp) in the current Seagull.
2026 BYD Seagull EV interior (Source: BYD)
We will have to wait closer to launch to learn battery specs and more details, but the upgraded Seagull will likely be equipped with BYD’s new Blade Batteries and Flash Charging tech.
The current 2026 Seagull is available with two battery packs: 30.08 kWh and 38.88 kWh. The former provides a CLTC range of up to 305 km (190 miles), and the latter, 405 km (251 miles).

title: Tesla FSD v14 swerved and try to drive me into a ditch for no reason
content:
Full Self-Driving (FSD)
Fred Lambert
| Aug 17 2026 - 7:14 am PT
Tesla’s Full Self-Driving v14.3.6 tried to take a highway exit that my car had already passed, at 110 km/h (68 mph), and it would have taken us straight into the ditch.
I was ready to take control, and I did, but it was scary. My girlfriend, sitting in the passenger seat, screamed in fear.
What the dashcam shows
This was Sunday night on Autoroute 55 in Quebec’s Mauricie region, running FSD (Supervised) v14.3.6 — the latest and greatest Tesla FSD build on the latest hardware.
The car is cruising at 110 km/h in the right lane. Dry pavement, no traffic in either direction, fresh painted lines, reflective overhead signage. Perfect conditions for FSD. As we pass under the gantry for exit 217, the right turn signal comes on and the car starts pulling toward the shoulder, still showing “Self-Driving” on the screen.
The problem is that the ramp was already peeling off behind us. It was going to drive us straight into the ditch by turning this late at that speed.
The speed readout goes 110, 109, 107, 104 as it commits to the maneuver. That’s when I grabbed the wheel. “Self-Driving” drops off the display at 102 km/h.
This wasn’t a lane-position wobble or a moment of hesitation. The car decided to put its blinker on and take an exit it had no business taking
These were ideal conditions for FSD
If you were designing the easiest possible scenario for Tesla’s system, this was it.
Divided highway. Night, so oncoming headlights and lane reflectors are easy to pick out. Zero traffic to reason about. Crisp lane markings. Big, well-lit signage.
Based on everything I’ve seen from v14, highway driving at night on an empty road is where the system is at its absolute best. I’ve done thousands of kilometres of exactly this without touching anything. Which is why I was confident. And that confidence is the whole trap.
I wrote about this exact risk in June
Two and a half months ago I published a piece arguing that
FSD v14 is so good it’s making me dangerously complacent
. I wrote then that “a system that works
perfectly creates a trap — drivers trust it just enough to stop paying attention, but it still fails unpredictably and sometimes critically.”
I stand by every word, and Sunday night was the demonstration. A couple thousand miles between critical interventions is genuinely impressive engineering. It’s also exactly the interval that teaches your brain to stop scanning.
Tesla’s own v14.3.6 release notes say the company “upgraded the Reinforcement Learning (RL) stage of training the FSD neural network,” rewrote the AI compiler with MLIR for “20% faster reaction time,” and improved the car’s response to system degradations, “reducing unnecessary disengagements.” Disengagements go down when the software gets better, and they also go down when the driver stops intervening. Tesla doesn’t publish anything that lets outsiders tell those two apart.
And the public numbers that do exist aren’t reassuring. Tesla reported
a record 207 Autopilot and FSD crashes to NHTSA in a single month
, with the narrative redacted on 99.9% of its 3,763 driver-assist crash reports since 2019. Musk is still telling investors that
unsupervised FSD will be widespread in the US by year-end
Waymo’s co-CEO keeps explaining why camera-only self-driving falls short
of what a driverless system actually needs.
Electrek’s Take
One near-miss is an anecdote, not data, but I think it’s an important reminder to stay attentive.
As I have often said, Tesla FSD v14 is a truly impressive product. Sure, it falls apart when compared to what FSD was originally sold as: becoming unsupervised self-driving. It’s not close to that and might never be. That will remain a problem and probably the worst move Tesla has ever done.
But if you set that aside and look at FSD as a point-to-point driver-assist system, it is truly incredible.
However, it is so incredible now that it breeds complacency. Tesla doesn’t help with CEO Elon Musk saying things like “you can look at your phone now while using it.”
This is obviously reckless. As the system gets better, Tesla needs to get better at convincing drivers to pay attention because of this complacency issue. Not the other way around.

title: Hyundai opens IONIQ 3 EV orders, starting at about $30,000
content:
Peter Johnson
| Aug 17 2026 - 6:57 am PT
opened orders for the IONIQ 3, its new entry-level electric hatch, starting at about $30,000.
Hyundai opens IONIQ 3 orders in the UK and Europe
The IONIQ 3 has received “the highest-ever level of customer interest recorded for a new Hyundai model,”
the company said
last month. That includes gas and electric vehicles.
Hyundai opened orders for the new electric hatch in the UK on Monday, its first compact EV from the IONIQ lineup.
It’s available in four trims: Advance, Premium, Ultimate, and N Line Evo, with standard and extended-range battery options.
The base Hyundai IONIQ 3 Advance trim with the standard 42 kWh battery starts at £22,245, or roughly $30,000. Upgrading to the larger 61 kWh battery starts at £25,745 ($35,000).
Ashley Andrew, President of Hyundai and Genesis UK, said the IONIQ 3 “delivers genuine EV innovation at a price point that makes electric mobility attainable for even more households.”
The Standard trim comes with the 42 kWh battery, offering a WLTP range of up to 213 miles, while the Premium, Ultimate, and N-Line Evo are powered by the 61 kWh battery, which provides up to 308 miles of range.
Hyundai IONIQ 3 (Source: Hyundai)
While it’s positioned as a little sibling to the IONIQ 5, the IONIQ 3 brings a new look to the lineup with Hyundai’s Art of Steel design language.
The new Aero Hatch shape “reimagines the compact EV silhouette,” Hyundai said, delivering a best-in-class drag coefficient of just 0.263. The design is not only extremely aerodynamic, but it also opens up the interior.
Hyundai IONIQ 3 (Source: Hyundai)
Measuring 4,155 mm (163.5″) in length, 1,800 mm (70.9″) in width, and 1,505 mm (59.3″) in height, with a wheelbase of 2,680 mm (105.5″), the IONIQ 3 is even slightly smaller than the Kia EV3 and Chevy Bolt EV.
Despite its compact size, the IONIQ 3 has smart storage throughout the interior, including a “Megabox” underfloor storage.
Hyundai IONIQ 3 interior (Source: Hyundai)
With a total boot capacity of up to 441 liters, Hyundai said the IONIQ 3 “sets the benchmark in the segment.”
The IONIQ 3 is Hyundai’s first vehicle in Europe and the UK that’s equipped with its new Pleos Connect infotainment system and software.
Hyundai IONIQ 3 interior with Pleos Connect infotainment system (Source: Hyundai)
Based on Android Automotive OS, the system is more like using a smartphone with apps and customizable screens, similar to what Tesla uses. It’s available with a 12.9″ or 14.6″ center infotainment screen and an optional driver display.
Other features include Hyundai Digital Key 2, Plug & Charge, an integrated EV route planner, and Vehicle-to-Load (V2L) functionality.

With DC fast charging, the IONIQ 3 can still recharge from 10% to 80% in about 29 minutes with the standard (42.2 kWh) battery. The long-range (61 kWh) battery takes around 30 minutes.
Hyundai is also opening IONIQ 3 orders in Europe. In
the Netherlands
, IONIQ 3 prices start at €27,995 ($32,000). It’s available with the same battery pack options (42 kWh or 61 kWh) and six trims: Select, Trend, Vision, N-Line, Prime, and N-Line Evo.

Hyundai expects IONIQ 3 models will begin arriving in showrooms in late September. Last Friday, the company
began IONIQ 3 production
at its Izmit plant in Turkey.
The facility will initially produce 30,000 IONIQ 3 vehicles annually. Next year, Hyundai will begin production of the next-generation BAYON and i20.
Electrek’s Take
Another affordable, practical electric vehicle that those in the US will miss out on. The IONIQ 3 is designed and built in Europe for the European market.
On top of that, the Trump Administration’s tariffs would make it too costly to import. Hyundai does offer the IONIQ 5, which is still among the most affordable (
and most popular
) EVs in the US, starting at $35,000. Unlike the IONIQ 3, which is made in Europe, Hyundai builds the IONIQ 5 at its Metaplant outside of Savannah, GA, for the US, enabling it to offer it at lower prices.
Hyundai’s sister company, Kia, also announced last week that
prices for the 2027 EV3
start at just $29,890 in the US.

title: Not sold on Tesla Powerwall? There are some great home battery alternatives out there
content:
Between increasingly extreme weather, rising electricity demands, and the rapid expansion of data centers, energy independence is starting to look less like a talking point for doomsday preppers and more like sound planning. That shift in thinking is driving more homeowners than ever towards solar-plus-battery energy solutions like the industry-leading Tesla Powerwall – but Powerwall isn’t the only game in town, anymore.
Maybe you’re avoiding Tesla products because of Elon Musk’s political antics, or maybe it’s Tesla’s recent recalls that have given you pause, or maybe you just want to see what else is out there. Whatever the reason, there are more compelling home battery options than ever – and they’ve got enough high-tech features packed into ’em that keeping the lights on in a storm might be the least interesting thing they can do.
As I was putting this list together, I realized there were plenty of ways for me to present this list. “Best batteries ..?” Too opinion-based. “Cheapest batteries ..?” Too much research and a quick descent into Temu-grade nonsense. In the end, I went with the same solution I’ve been using on my 0% EV financing lists: alphabetical order, by brand.
Anker SOLIX X1
The Anker SOLIX X1 is built to be highly modular. Starting out with a relatively modest 5 kWh of energy storage from a single low-profile LiFePO4 battery, the X1 system allows owners to stack storage and scale up all the way up to 180 kWh. That flexibility makes it a particularly interesting option for homeowners who are sold on the concept of a home battery but not quite sure how far down the rabbit hole they want to go. With Anker SOLIX X1, they can meet their most critical needs on day one, and build up to a system that can support their wants later.
The X1 also adds some thoughtful backup features, including automatic storm preparation and a 20 millisecond automative switchover time, while its IP66-rated weatherproof enclosure and 10-year warranty are reassuring for something that’s supposed to sit outside and keep your house running when the grid doesn’t.
BLUETTI EP800
The portable power experts at BLUETTI have put together another modular home battery system built around the company’s EP800 inverter and modular B500 battery packs. A basic two-battery configuration provides 9.92 kWh of storage, while additional packs can push total capacity to nearly 40 kWh and 7.6 kW of output.
The EP800 can work with rooftop solar panels or microinverters, but BLUETTI designed it to also be able to charge from the grid during cheaper off-peak hours, stockpiling that energy for when rates rise. That means you get backup power and time-of-use savings without needing rooftop solar, making the EP800 a compelling case for renters or homeowners who aren’t quite ready to make the jump to a full solar-plus-storage system.
Enphase IQ Battery 5P
If you’re looking for a one-brand solution for EV charging and whole-home battery backup but don’t want to be “locked in” to GM or Tesla’s ecosystem, Enphase offers a full line of battery solutions that might be what you’re looking for.
Described as a full off-grid system, Enphase batteries let homeowners power their homes without a utility connection, even for extended periods. It works by combining the Enphase IQ Battery 5P with IQ8 series microinverters with Sunlight JumpStart, and a third-party standby AC generator.
“Energy systems developer Enphase Energy is providing an even more holistic approach to managing home power usage with the introduction of new EV charger technology called the IQ line,” wrote Scooter doll, when the brand first introduced its EV charging solutions back in 2023. “The Enphase IQ is Wi-Fi enabled and integrates seamlessly into a customer’s existing home system that can be controlled with your phone.”
FranklinWH aPower S
Fans of the Tesla Powerwall often point to its sleek, integrated design as one of the things that’s most appealing about it. The FranklinWH aPower S takes a similarly clean, minimalist approach, packing the battery and inverter into a single unit and simplifying installation. Each aPower S unit stores 15 kWh of usable energy and can deliver up to 10 kW of continuous power, while multiple aPower batteries can be combined for larger homes or higher energy needs.
The aPower S can also be wired into existing solar installations and be controlled virtually as part of a larger VPP scheme, making it a particularly flexible option for homeowners who already have solar and simply to add storage to their existing solution.
We got a chance to speak with FranklinWH CEO Gary Lam about the scalability of his home battery solutions. You can check out that episode, above.
GM Energy Home System
Arguably the most fully integrated EV + battery backup + solar option out there, the GM Energy Home System promises to do everything a conventional home solar battery does, plus the ability work seamlessly with your GM EV to provide even more flexibility and energy independence – whether that means using the electric fuel stored in your EV to hold out that much longer in an emergency, or using the energy stored in your home’s solar battery to power an escape in your electric Chevrolet is up to you.
GM Energy and GM’s car dealers list Qmerit as their installation partner. They’re great, but if you already “have a guy,” you can order the 10.6 kWh Home System directly from GM Energy’s website for as little as $11,897 (as I type this).
Sigenergy V2X
As some of the earliest and most enthusiastic EV adopters, Tesla fans have also been among the loudest advocates for using the energy stored their cars’ batteries to back up their homes — or even the grid itself. Unfortunately for them, the slow-selling Cybertruck is the only Tesla vehicle that officially supports bi-directional charging. If you’re one of the many Model 3 and Y owners frustrated by those delays, there’s good news: those vehicles are now capable of V2H charging thanks to an “impressive” Powerwall competitor, Sigenergy.
The good news doesn’t stop with the Tesla cars, however. The Sigenergy V2X also works with a number of popular EV models over the DIN70121 protocol, and several VW/Audi/Porsche and Mercedes-Benz models over the ISO15118-2 protocol.
Our Editor-in-Chief, Fred Lambert, recently went on a Sigenergy deep dive with Sylvain Juteau, President of Roulez Electrique, and came away deeply impressed with the system. I’ve included the video, above, and you can read more about the system itself at this link
Villara VillaGrid+
I’m not an electrician, a chemical engineer, or someone who’s researched thousands of home battery installations. That’s why this isn’t a “best batteries” post, after all – but our friends and solar industry experts at EnergySage, though? They’re all three of those things, and they really, really like the Villara VillaGrid+.
“The Villara VillaGrid+ stands out as the best battery on the market, scoring highest in EnergySage’s rigorous Equipment Rating System, explains EnergySage’s Kristina Zagame. “That said, (the Villara VillaGrid+) is not necessarily the best Tesla Powerwall alternative. It’s a very different (and much pricier) battery.”
What makes the VillaGrid+ worth the price premium? According to Zagame, it all comes down to the battery’s lithium-titanium-oxide, or LTO chemistry. “Unlike more traditional lithium-ion batteries, LTO has better recharge capabilities for longer life cycles, and doesn’t contain any carbon, which makes it extra safe. The downside is you’ll definitely shell out more money upfront for the VillaGrid+.”
Top comment by joegoesbananas
I have a triple-Powerwall and solar setup installed by Tesla, and I highly recommend buying an alternative product. The Tesla batteries themselves aren't the problem, it's their inverter/gateway design. We are on our second inverter (already also dying; first one lasted less than a year), and our second gateway. Tesla designed the inverters with zero airflow. There is a small fan inside and a tiny grill, but the grill is at the bottom, is comically small, and the fan doesn't point at it, so no hot air can escape. The fan screams while it recirculates trapped scorching air until the inverter repeatedly turns off due to overheating, and eventually fails completely. You have to prop the cover open if you don't want to lose DC power sources every time the weather goes over 95 degrees (and my unit is north-facing and is completely shaded). When your system dies, expect at least a month before they will fix it, and that's after they ignore you, argue with you, don't call back, make you do the same troubleshooting steps multiple times, etc. For a system that one buys to reduce worry and stress, our Tesla Powerwall system has caused us an awful lot of worry and stress.
That extra money will also buy some additional peace of mind, as Villara backs its LTO batteries with a 20-year warranty compared to Tesla Powerwall and its (and just about everyone else’s) 10-year deal. I couldn’t find a price, but Villara’s other products, like VillaGrid 5.75 kWh battery, come in at nearly double the Powerwall’s per kWh cost.

| Aug 17 2026 - 5:06 am PT
GM’s Latin American expansion continues with news that Chevrolet is offering EV buyers free charging at network at dealerships throughout Peru, where sales of plug-powered vehicles are growing rapidly.
The General is putting serious money into its global EV expansion these days,
with a high-profile launch of the Cadillac brand in South America’s largest car market

People like them
Chevy Captiva (left), and Spark EV (right); via GM Authority.
“In the first half of the year, sales of electrified vehicles grew by more than 86 percent in Peru, demonstrating increased consumer interest in these technologies,” said Marketing Manager of GM Peru, Melisa Black. “However, this progress must also be accompanied by more charging options. That translates to an impressive 8,285 plug-in Chevrolets sold in Peru during the first half of the year
, alone – with more to come as the company continues its push into the region with more affordable,
sometimes Chinese-derived EVs

No charging sign, by Steve Birkett.

title: Agastya Energy plans 12 GW ingot, wafer factory in India - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Agastya Energy plans to invest INR 78 billion ($815.8 million) to develop a 12 GW ingot and wafer manufacturing facility in Kurnool, Andhra Pradesh. The project will complement its planned 5 GW cell and module manufacturing capacity and strengthen India’s integrated solar supply chain.
Uma Gupta
17 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Agastya Energy recently held a ceremony marking the start of the next phase of its growth.
| Agastya Green Energy
Agastya Green Energy Ltd, part of the Anubhav Agarwal Group (AAG), plans to develop an integrated 12 GW ingot and wafer manufacturing facility in the Orvakal Industrial Area in Kurnool, Andhra Pradesh, with an estimated investment of INR 78 billion ($815.8 million).
The facility will have 12 GW each of ingot and wafer manufacturing capacity, complementing the company’s planned solar cell and module manufacturing operations.
Agastya Energy told
pv magazine
that it is planning 5 GW of solar cell and module manufacturing capacity in two phases. The first phase will comprise 2 GW of cell and module capacity. The company said it will review the remaining capacity in line with future demand, while evaluating opportunities for both vertical and horizontal expansion.
“Our INR 7,800 crore investment in Agastya Energy reflects our long-term conviction in India’s energy transition and our commitment to building globally competitive manufacturing capabilities at scale,” said AAG Chairman Anubhav Agarwal. “We believe that strengthening domestic manufacturing will be critical to meeting India’s growing energy needs, reducing import dependence and creating a resilient energy ecosystem for the decades ahead.”
“The expansion into ingot and wafer manufacturing marks a critical upstream pillar of Agastya Energy’s integrated solar manufacturing strategy, complementing our solar cell and module capabilities and strengthening our end-to-end PV value chain,” said Piyush Bichhoriya, director of Agastya Energy. “It will deepen our presence across the solar ecosystem, drive greater domestic value addition, and create synergies across manufacturing, IPP and EPC.”
“The global energy transition is creating a strong need for resilient, scalable and globally competitive solar manufacturing. This expansion will strengthen Agastya Energy’s capabilities across ingots, wafers, cells and modules. It marks an important step towards establishing India as a leading hub for clean energy manufacturing,” added Agastya Energy CEO Bernhard Rack.
The integrated facility will bring together ingot, wafer, cell and module manufacturing, enabling greater manufacturing efficiency and integration across the upstream and downstream segments of the photovoltaic value chain.
Agastya Energy’s ingot and wafer expansion comes as India’s Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) expands the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) framework to include ingots and wafers. The move is aimed at strengthening supply chains, reducing import dependence and improving quality across the solar value chain.
The ALMM requirement for solar wafers will take effect on June 1, 2028.

title: Solar crosses 3 TW threshold - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Global solar capacity has surpassed 3 TW, with China driving much of the recent expansion and emerging markets increasingly contributing to growth. As deployment accelerates, grid infrastructure, energy storage, and demand flexibility will become critical to integrating the next wave of solar capacity.
Alessandra Neris
17 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Image: qimono / Pixabay
The world surpassed 3 TW of installed solar capacity, marking another milestone in the rapid expansion of photovoltaic energy.
According to BloombergNEF (BNEF), it took about 10 years for global solar capacity to rise from 100 GW in 2012 to 1 TW. The second terawatt was added in less than three years, while the third came less than two years later. The exact date of the 3 TW milestone varies, however, depending on the methodology and database used by analysts.
The pace of expansion is expected to accelerate further. BNEF projects that global solar capacity will exceed 9 TW by 2036, putting the latest milestone into perspective against the growth expected over the next decade.
China remains the leading force
The geography of solar expansion has shifted significantly during this period. According to Bloomberg, developed countries accounted for most of the first terawatt, supported by incentive programs designed to accelerate solar adoption.
China emerged as the main driver of growth during the second and third terawatts. The country combined rapid deployment of solar capacity with large-scale manufacturing, helping to reduce technology costs and support adoption in other markets.
Solar expansion is also reaching countries that previously accounted for only a small share of the global market. Pakistan, Nigeria, and the Philippines have recorded strong growth, particularly in rooftop solar. Smaller markets, including Cuba and Lebanon, have also experienced rapid expansion.
As a result, the number of countries with significant solar markets has increased. According to BNEF, 74 countries had at least 1 GW of installed solar capacity in 2025, up from 42 in 2020.
Expansion remains concentrated
Despite broader adoption, solar deployment remains concentrated in a relatively small number of markets. The share of poorer countries in new solar installations has remained virtually unchanged since 2020, while China has consolidated its position as the primary driver of global growth.
BNEF expects this trend to change in the coming years. Its projections indicate that the share of developing countries in new installations will begin to increase from 2026. By 2036, more than a quarter of global installed solar capacity is expected to be located in developing countries, while the share held by wealthy countries is projected to fall to around 20%.
Grid and storage take center stage
The rapid growth in installed capacity is creating new challenges for power systems. In China, solar deployment has outpaced the expansion of infrastructure needed to transmit and store electricity.
As a result, the country is experiencing rising levels of curtailment, with some solar generation being reduced during periods of high output. A slowdown in new Chinese installations is expected as the country shifts its focus toward integrating renewable generation and expanding the capacity needed to consume it.
Energy storage is becoming increasingly important in this transition. Lithium-ion batteries can absorb excess electricity during periods of peak solar generation and discharge it later, including after sunset.
According to BNEF, energy storage capacity will be a decisive factor in the next phase of solar expansion. Without sufficient storage, fully utilizing additional solar capacity will become increasingly difficult.
The 3 TW milestone shows that solar has moved beyond niche technology status and become a central component of global power-capacity expansion. The challenge in the next phase, however, will be different.
As photovoltaic generation continues to grow, transmission, storage, and demand flexibility will become increasingly important alongside the deployment of new modules. The ability to use solar electricity at the right time and in the right place will be crucial to turning growth in installed capacity into effectively utilized generation.

title: When solar is sold by AI agents - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Wave Sales says its new AI voice agents can increase customer satisfaction and cut installer soft costs by helping to guide home solar customers through a multi-month installation process using the company’s proprietary memory layer and industry-specific integrations.
Ben Zientara
17 Aug 2026
Technology & Products
Energy Storage
Residential
Software
Image: Kindel Media on Pexels
Residential solar installers face a challenging reality: with the sunset of the Section 25D tax credit at the end of 2025, margins on cash sales are smaller than ever, and working with third-party ownership (TPO) financing providers adds complexity to all facets of the business, including sales, design and installation.
The additional work of complying with TPO record keeping processes also involves other businesses in the solar industry, like module manufacturers and distributors. Maintaining compliance with domestic content requirements and restrictions on doing business with foreign entities of concern require precise levels of materials management and inventory control that are well suited to an automated system.
A new startup called Wave Sales is now offering an agentic AI platform that aims to address those issues and more: streamlining and adding value to the residential solar sales process, providing integrations with other popular platforms and planned future interfaces with distribution, finance, permitting and more.
Wave Sales is the creation of co-founders Colin Walsh and Vu Nguyen. Walsh brings years of experience in residential solar lending and lead generation through his time at Wave Solar, SolarReviews and Mosaic. Nguyen brings over a decade of experience building AI agents at places like Google and Capital One.
Walsh also previously served as the chief revenue officer at Amara NZero, parent company of solar distributor Sungry Solar, whose CEO Neel Desai is on board with Wave Sales as an advisor and customer.
In addition to Sunrgy, the company’s early customers include solar and energy storage installers across the United States. While its platform is specially designed with the solar sector in mind, Wave Sales is also taking on other home services providers like HVAC and roofing companies as customers.
Winning over sales teams
While internal sales staff are often initially skeptical of automation because of fears the AI might take their leads (if not their jobs), Walsh says early adopters have quickly come to view the system as a collaborative teammate.
“You can build trust in a low-risk way with your team where they see it as an assistant, and actually, they start referring to it by name,” Walsh says. “’Sunny helped me close that deal’ or ‘Sunny booked an appointment on the calendar.’ The assistant becomes kind of like a teammate. You can throw more work at the teammate… it’s like a multiplier as you gain trust in the system”.
At one early customer, team members were wary of the AI until the agent began qualifying inbound web leads and live-transferring close-ready deals directly to representatives. Walsh notes that sales reps rapidly embrace the platform once they see it doing things like reviving stalled leads, recovering no-shows and capturing business during nights and weekends.
Another way of building a human-to-bot camaraderie with customers is through the customization options available. Clients can choose one of 3,000 available voices — or even use a custom voice print.
Desta Rudolph, CEO of early customer Independent Energy, says the custom voice print is an essential tool in Hawaii, where his company installs residential and commercial solar.
“This isn’t our first experience trying an AI agent,” Rudolph explained in a video interview with Wave Sales. “When people heard that voice that our [old] agent had, they hung up immediately. There’s a way that people speak in Hawaii. We have a very particular way of saying things in places: street names; city names. And to have that very, very local, genuine sounding voice…I was sold at the point that I heard its voice.”
The memory layer
Wave Sales says its technology addresses the limitations of standard AI bots by using a proprietary memory layer to maintain important information about customers. Walsh explained that most AI bots reset after a single interaction, losing context if a call drops or escalates.
Wave Sales attempts to solve this with a proprietary memory layer designed for agents that act autonomously over time. This means the agent remembers its previous interactions with a caller. In the case of a residential solar customer, the agent maintains details about the progress on their installation.
During the months-long process of a home solar installation, the agent that booked an initial appointment can later answer customer questions about permitting or post-installation warranties, using the full context of the project history without requiring the customer to repeat themselves. And if that customer calls back in the future to seek customer support, the agent will have the information it needs to ensure their needs are met quickly.
Solar-specific integrations
Walsh says Wave Sales is working on connections with industry-specific tools to help streamline operational workflows. The company recently signed a partnership with OpenSolar to explore integrations that allow agents to perform actions within users’ workspaces, such as looking up projects and accelerating the pre-appointment quoting process.
“We’re excited to partner with Wave Sales and introduce OpenSolar Pros to AI Agent services,” says Andrew McGuigan, general manager of the Americas at OpenSolar. “As installers look for new ways to improve efficiency and customer experience, AI services like these can help free up teams to focus on increasing sales and growing their business.”
Additionally, the company has held discussion with Google about using its Solar API to detect existing arrays from satellite imagery. The integration could provide installer teams with a way to target their response to inquiries toward offering service or repairs and selling add-ons like battery storage to customers with existing solar.
The agent-to-agent future
Looking ahead, Walsh predicts a shift in how homeowners procure these services, from manual web searches and phone calls toward tasks delegated to personal AI assistants. Wave Sales aims to be the booking gateway for this exchange.
“There’s inevitably going to be a world in the future where agents are booking home services appointments in addition to humans,” Walsh says. He imagines a future in which a human might start a transaction by saying something to their own AI agent like “Hey, I need to install solar in my house, and I want you to find me the best-rated solar installer that’s near me.”
In that situation, the Wave Sales agent would be the intermediary between the homeowner’s agent and the installer (or installers), managing rules about calendar availability, service performance and more to give validated results back to the agent that originates the request.
“That’s the future of this tool,” Walsh said. “It’ll be able to communicate with both humans and personal AI assistants, [connecting] agents that need tasks done with all the folks in the clean energy industry. We’re aiming to be the agent-to-agent layer within the clean energy industry.”

title: New Zealand to simplify small, medium-sized solar installations - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The New Zealand government is moving ahead with a series of recommendations designed to simplify installing small- and medium-sized solar systems, including plans to legalize plug-in solar.
Patrick Jowett
17 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Commercial & industrial
Residential
Image: Vivint Solar/Unsplash
The government of New Zealand has agreed to move ahead with recommendations laid out in a recent
sector review report
covering small- and medium-sized solar installations for residential and commercial customers.
The 15 recommendations outlined in the report include previously-announced plans to
legalize plug-in solar
, as well as approving installations under 10 kW by the next working day and allowing accredited installers to sign off on an installation less than 100 kW in size without an inspection.
Other measures include creating a standardized process for connecting solar installations to electricity distributors, publishing consumer-friendly information about electricity meters and improving retailer processes and communications.
The country’s regulation minister, David Seymour, and its energy minister, Simeon Brown, commented that adopting the recommendations will make installing small- or medium-sized solar systems in New Zealand “the simplest in the developed world.”
“New Zealanders want more control over their power bills and making it easier to connect solar is one way to do that by allowing people to make use of the free sunshine that lands on their property,” Brown said. “We’re already seeing increasing rooftop connections so, logically, the more the hassle and cost can be reduced, the greater the uptake will be.”
He added that the adoption of plug-in solar will be “a game change for people who rent” as it will allow people to take their solar system with them when they move.
Previous analysis released by the Ministry for Regulation suggested that implementing the recommendations in the report would take the average installation approval for residential solar from around NZD 640 ($375.99) and three months to NZD 200 and six days. It added that the recommendations could deliver net benefits of between NZD 28 million and NZD 50 million over ten years through lower compliance costs, reduced delays and the use of plug-in solar.
In April, New Zealand’s electricity authority introduced a
10 kW default export limit
for residential solar and battery systems in a move designed to standardize grid access.
New Zealand’s cumulative solar capacity stood at 836 MW at the end of last year, according to figures from the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA). Its largest solar farm to date, a
150 MW site
on the country’s north island, came online in July.

title: Energy storage cell shipment data for H1 2026 reveal three structural shifts - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
In the first half of 2026, global energy storage cell shipments reached 467.84 GWh, up 94.8% year on year, just one data point from InfoLink Consulting, which examines each of these shifts in turn.
Corrine Lin
17 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
bateria de íons de sódio desenvolvida pela Hithium | Imagem: Hithium
In the first half of 2026 (H1), global energy storage cell shipments reached 467.84 GWh, up 94.8% year-on-year. Quarterly shipments exceeded 200 GWh for the third consecutive quarter, with second-quarter shipments reaching a record 262 GWh. Shipments to markets outside China totaled nearly 250 GWh in H1, accounting for more than half of the global total.
The headline figures hide structural shifts. Three developments have occurred during H1, including a reshuffling of the competitive landscape, a new normal marked by a persistently tight supply-demand balance amid the rapid iteration of cell formats, and a rebound in the share of shipments to markets outside China to above 50%. InfoLink Consulting examines each of these shifts in turn.
The ten largest suppliers’ combined share of global energy storage cell shipments (CR10) has fallen steadily over the past year, from 91.2% in H1 2025 to 88.8% for full-year 2025, 85.2% in the first quarter of 2026 (Q1), and 82.3% in H1 2026. The nearly 9-percentage-point year-on-year decline marks the sharpest drop in recent years.
The decline is more due to the dynamics of a supply-constrained market than any seasonal variations. Once capacity at leading manufacturers is fully committed, incremental demand spills over to mid-tier suppliers. Once these suppliers pass customer qualification and establish a delivery track record, the market share they gain will not automatically revert to the market leaders.
CATL, Hithium, EVE Energy, BYD Energy Storage, and CALB retained the top five positions, although their combined share (CR5) fell to 56.5%. Meanwhile, emerging players such as Sunwoda and Ganfeng LiEnergy are also gaining ground, with several challengers now ranked 11th to 15th and making a strong push into the top 10. The competitive landscape is becoming less concentrated at the top as mid-tier manufacturers accelerate their expansion.
However, as large-capacity cells enter mass production, leading manufacturers could see their market share return to an upward trajectory, supported by consistent product quality, economies of scale, and stronger pricing advantages across their sales channels.
*Source: InfoLink’s Global Energy Storage Supply Chain Database
The 314 Ah cell has remained in tight supply for nearly a year, with prices rising by more than 15% over the past six months. Meanwhile, the penetration rate of 500 Ah and larger cells in the utility-scale storage market exceeded 10% in H1 2026.
The 500-Ah-and-above segment now features multiple competing formats, including 587 Ah, 588 Ah, 648 Ah, 684 Ah, and 702 Ah, and even cells exceeding 1,000 Ah. For cell manufacturers, choosing a format that fails to gain market adoption can prove far more costly than waiting to see which format becomes the industry standard.
The solar PV industry has seen a similar pattern before. The rapid evolution of energy storage cell formats closely resembles the rivalry between 182 mm and 210 mm that emerged after a period of rapid changes in PV wafer sizes. There is no clear technical winner. Instead, the cost of adapting the broader supply chain determines how quickly the market converges on a standard. Until then, established cell formats will still retain a high market share in the near term.
At this stage, 587 Ah and 588 Ah energy storage cells remain the main focus of capacity expansion, although manufacturers are still proceeding cautiously amid widespread wait-and-see sentiment. Progress on production lines for formats such as 648 Ah warrants close attention. In residential storage, meanwhile, the market is rapidly shifting from 100 Ah to 314 Ah cells, with the combined penetration rate of 280 Ah and 314 Ah cells approaching 30%. In H2, the adoption of 392 Ah cells in the residential storage market will be worth watching, as some manufacturers push the transition from 314 Ah to 392 Ah cells.
Based on H1 shipment data, book-to-bill (B/B) ratios that have remained above 1.2 for several consecutive months at a number of manufacturers, and continued export front-loading ahead of Q4, InfoLink expects the tight supply-demand balance to persist through H2, with new capacity unlikely to ramp up quickly enough to offset demand pulled forward by policy.
Accordingly, InfoLink has raised its forecast for global energy storage cell shipments in 2026 to 1,026 GWh, marking the second upward revision this year. Compared with shipments of 612.39 GWh in 2025, the new forecast represents growth of around 67.5% year on year.
With 467.84 GWh already shipped in H1, the revised forecast leaves around 558 GWh for H2. With manufacturers operating at full capacity and selling all their output, and B/B ratios remaining elevated, InfoLink considers this a relatively conservative trajectory. The forecast rests on three assumptions: ramp-up losses as production lines transition to large-capacity cell production, a seasonal decline in global demand in Q4, and an export rush toward year end that is expected to show up primarily in customs clearance volumes rather than additional production.
Energy storage cell shipments to markets outside China reached 248.73 GWh in H1, accounting for around 53.2% of global shipments.
Changes to China’s export tax rebates were a key factor shaping shipments during the period. Readers in the PV industry will already be familiar with the first part of the policy announced by China’s Ministry of Finance and State Taxation Administration on Jan. 9: export tax rebates for PV products were eliminated from April 1, 2026. Energy storage batteries, however, followed a more gradual phaseout schedule. The rebate rate was reduced from 9% to 6% from April 1 through Dec. 31, 2026, before being eliminated entirely on Jan. 1, 2027.
The different timelines have produced very different patterns. PV manufacturers rushed to export in Q1 before the rebate was eliminated, and the rush largely ran its course within the quarter. For energy storage batteries, the phaseout stretches across the year. Suppliers accelerated shipments in Q1 ahead of the reduction from 9% to 6%, but a 6% rebate remained in place from April onward, with full elimination taking effect on Jan. 1, 2027. This explains why the cell market saw no seasonal slowdown in H1.
The U.S., however, has not been the main source of this latest growth. Quite the opposite: import restrictions tightened further in H1. The Section 301 tariff increase took effect during the period, raising the tariff rate applicable to Chinese-made battery energy storage system (BESS) products from 7.5% to 25%. Combined with other duties, the overall tariff rate climbed as high as 48.4% at one point and currently stands at around 40.9%. Tariff and non-tariff barriers operate in tandem, with measures such as Federal Communications Commission (FCC) requirements and foreign entity of concern (FEOC) restrictions imposing greater practical constraints on the industry than tariffs themselves.
The resulting supply gap in the U.S. is being filled by South Korean manufacturers. LG Energy Solution (LGES) has begun mass production of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells for energy storage at its facility in Holland, Michigan, and plans to expand capacity from 17 GWh to 30 GWh in 2026. The shift is also visible in the rankings. LGES ranked tenth in utility-scale storage cell shipments and eighth in shipments to markets outside China, with its market share rising quarter by quarter since Q2 2025. This is broadly in line with InfoLink’s Q1 expectation that South Korean manufacturers would return to the global top 10.
Beyond the U.S., the rising share of shipments to markets outside China is being driven primarily by Europe’s storage deployment targets and policy support, growth in both utility-scale and distributed storage in Australia, large-scale projects across Latin America and the Middle East, and emerging markets such as India, Brazil, and Southeast Asia that are moving from initial market formation into a more meaningful phase of deployment.
Viewed through the lens of the PV industry’s development, each of these three shifts has a familiar precedent. Concentration in the midstream supply chain eased during periods of rapid capacity expansion. Product formats evolved quickly along multiple tracks before standards began to converge. Demand was also clearly front-loaded around policy step-downs.
The difference is speed. It took the PV industry nearly a decade to move through these stages. Energy storage appears to be compressing a similar transition into just one or two years. That suggests many of the lessons learned from the PV industry remain relevant to energy storage, but the window for responding to market shifts has become much shorter. The first real test of whether those lessons still hold will come in 2027.
Corrine Lin
brings over a decade of expertise in renewable-energy research and market intelligence, spanning solar PV, energy storage, and the net-zero transition. As InfoLink’s Chief Analyst since its founding, she has led the team in delivering actionable industry insights. Since assuming the role of Chief Executive Officer of InfoLink Consulting on January 1, 2026, she has continued to advance the company’s research-driven strategy and advisory capabilities.

title: Kanion unveils residential monoblock outdoor heat pumps with 5.15 COP - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Kanion’s Deluxe Series R32 monobloc air-to-water heat pumps span 6 kW to 30 kW, with COP up to 5.15, SCOP up to 5.13, and water temperatures up to 65 C. The units operate from −25 C to 43 C, use R32 refrigerant and 3D DC inverter technology, and feature a corrosion-resistant outdoor heat-exchanger coating.
Emiliano Bellini
17 Aug 2026
Technology & Products
Heat pumps
Residential
Kanion Co’s Deluxe Series R32 monobloc air-to-water heat pump. | Image: Kanion
Chinese manufacturer Kanion has introduced its Deluxe Series of monobloc air-to-water heat pumps for residential and commercial heating, cooling and domestic hot water applications. The systems are available in capacities from 6 kW to 30 kW, with single- and three-phase configurations.
The new product line is positioned as a solution for residential and commercial buildings where space heating, cooling and hot-water production need to be combined in a single hydronic system. Its monobloc configuration keeps the refrigerant circuit within the outdoor unit, potentially simplifying installation compared with split heat-pump systems, according to the manufacturer.
The Kanion Co Deluxe Series R32 Mono air-to-water heat pump comprises single-phase models rated from 6 kW to 16 kW, while three-phase versions are available with capacities of 16 kW, 18 kW, 22 kW, 26 kW and 30 kW, according to technical specifications published by Kanion’s Greek distributor.
The single-phase units operate at 220–240 V and 50 Hz, while the three-phase models use a 380–415 V, 50 Hz supply. The systems use difluoromethane (R32) refrigerant and incorporate a 3D DC inverter, a Wilo circulator and what Kanion describes as “Green Fin” technology, which consists of a protective coating applied to the fins of the outdoor heat exchanger.
The coating is intended to improve the coil’s resistance to corrosion caused by moisture and other environmental exposure, while facilitating drainage from the heat-exchanger surface. This can be particularly relevant for outdoor installations exposed to humid, polluted or coastal environments. Kanion’s published material does not, however, provide detailed information on the coating’s chemical composition or quantify any resulting improvement in heat-exchanger lifetime.
For the single-phase range, the reported coefficient of performance (COP) reaches 5.15 for the 8 kW model, while COP values for the other modles range from 4.50 to 4.95. Seasonal coefficient of performance (SCOP) ranges from 4.53 to 5.13, while seasonal energy efficiency ratios (SEER) range from 4.62 to 5.87.
The three-phase units have COP values between 3.91 and 4.70 and SCOP values between 3.14 and 4.60, depending on model and operating conditions. Kanion lists an A+++ energy efficiency rating at a 35 C water temperature under warm-climate conditions.
The heat pumps are designed to operate at outdoor temperatures between −25 C and 43 C and can deliver water at temperatures of up to 65 C. This makes the series suitable for low-temperature heating systems as well as applications requiring higher water temperatures, although actual performance depends on operating conditions and system design, the company said.
The smallest single-phase models measure 1,295 mm × 792 mm × 429 mm, while larger units use dimensions of 1,385 mm × 945 mm × 526 mm. Sound power levels for the single-phase models range from 58 dB to 68 dB. The three-phase range reaches sound power levels of up to 77 dB for the 30 kW model.
The company offers a five-year warranty for the compressor and two years for other components.

title: Spain extends Almaraz nuclear plant operation through 2030 - pv magazine Global
content: Spain’s Official State Gazette (BOE) published on Friday, August 14, formally approved the renewal of the operating authorization for Spain’s Almaraz nuclear power plant Units I and II through June 8, 2030. The Ministry for the Ecological Transition (MITECO) described the measure as “a limited, short-term extension” that leaves the 2035 target for closing Spain’s nuclear fleet unchanged. Order TED/864/2026, dated August 12, extends Unit I’s operation by 31 months and Unit II’s by 19 months compared with their previously scheduled closure dates. The government said the decision reflects the current international energy environment, marked by the conflict in the Middle East and the war in Ukraine, and their impact on prices, volatility, and uncertainty in global gas markets. According to MITECO, temporarily maintaining Almaraz’s nuclear generation capacity could reduce the Spanish electricity system’s exposure to periods of high prices while renewable energy and storage capacity continue to expand. The ministry said the extension will not result in additional costs for consumers and argued that its temporary nature will provide firm generation capacity while solar PV, wind, and energy storage are deployed at a faster pace. From a regulatory perspective, the renewal follows a technical assessment by Spain’s Nuclear Safety Council (CSN), which has continuously monitored the plant’s operation and compliance with nuclear safety and radiological protection requirements. During the renewal process, the CSN requested additional information on issues including the management of aging in safety-related structures, systems, and components, as well as spent fuel management during the extended operating period. After reviewing the documentation submitted by the plant owners, the CSN issued a favorable report. Iberdrola , Endesa , and Naturgy , which jointly own Almaraz and had previously agreed to Spain’s phased nuclear shutdown plan, subsequently requested an extension of the plant’s operation. Iberdrola holds a 53% stake, Endesa 36%, and Naturgy 11%. Iberdrola and Endesa initially proposed extending the plant’s operation by 10 years. However, Naturgy opposed that proposal, and the requirement for unanimous approval among the owners ultimately led to a request for a more limited extension through 2030. The current nuclear shutdown schedule is based on a 2018 protocol signed by the plant owners and Enresa, Spain’s state-owned radioactive waste management company. The protocol established a phased closure of the country’s nuclear fleet between 2027 and 2035, with Almaraz scheduled to be the first plant to shut down. However, the protocol is non-binding, and Spanish regulations allow operators to apply for license renewals within established timeframes. The decision represents a departure from the nuclear closure timetable agreed by the Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) and left-winged party Sumar. The Almaraz extension has received support from political parties in Extremadura, municipalities surrounding the plant, and its owners. The renewal also comes as other Spanish nuclear plants approach key regulatory deadlines. The operating licenses for the Cofrentes and Ascó I plants are due to expire in the coming years, requiring their operators to initiate their own renewal procedures with the CSN. Meanwhile, researchers from the Barcelona School of Economics (BSE) and the Catalonia Institute for Energy Research (IREC) have concluded that extending the operating lives of Spain’s nuclear plants would make the country’s 2030 renewable electricity target under its National Energy and Climate Plan (PNIEC) unattainable. The study, titled “ A stochastic policy assessment of Spain’s 81% renewable electricity target for 2030 ,” was published in July in Energy for Sustainable Development . The post Spain extends Almaraz nuclear plant operation through 2030 appeared first on pv magazine Global .

title: Portugal installs 372 MW of solar in December-May - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Portugal’s total solar capacity is now estimated above 7 GW. While the country is one of Europe’s leading nations for renewable energy generation, the sector is facing substantial regulatory challenges that are forming barriers to future investment.
Patrick Jowett
17 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Portugal
Image: Den Harrson/Unsplash
Portugal added 372 MW of solar between December 2025 and May 2026, according to figures from the Portuguese Association Of Renewable Energy (APREN). The figure comprises 201 MW of decentralized generation and 171 MW of centralized solar power plants, the association added.
These additions take Portugal’s cumulative solar capacity to an estimated 7.3 GW when accounting for statistics published by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), which placed the country’s total solar capacity at 6.95 GW by the end of 2025.
Susana Serôdio, APREN’s Policy and Market Intelligence Coordinator, told
pv magazine
that 2026 has brought historic successes for Portugal’s solar market, particularly in July, when solar technology
led the country’s electricity production for the first time
But she added that the sector is facing substantial regulatory challenges that act as barriers to investment. “Licensing processes remain a critical bottleneck, currently taking between five and seven years in Portugal, a timeframe that far exceeds the acceleration targets set by the [EU’s] RED III Directive,” Serôdio explained.
A lack of new capacity auctions since 2022 and insufficient grid capacity also severely hinders the integration of new projects, Serôdio added, while Portugal remains that only European countries applying a permanent contribution on the net value of renewable energy assets via a tax known as the CESE (Contribuição Extraordinária sobre o Setor Energético). Serôdio said this mechanism results in a total tax burden representative of around 35% of companies’ profits.
Despite these challenges, Serôdio told
pv magazine
that Portugal’s wider energy market is being driven by robust performance in renewable generation and the resulting market competitiveness.
“During the first seven months of 2026, renewables accounted for 75.0% of the electricity generated in Portugal Continental, placing the country fourth among analyzed European nations for renewable electricity incorporation,” she explained. “This high share of renewables has directly influenced market prices, bringing the [Iberian electricity market] MIBEL average down to €57.30 ($66.47)/MWh between January and July, which represents a 10.0% decrease compared to the same period in 2025.”
Looking ahead, the future development of renewables in Portugal is expected to be heavily characterized by hybrid projects, Serôdio said, with around 80% of new projects currently under construction combining different renewable sources to take advantage of existing grid connection points.
Storage projects are also expected to play an increasing role in Portugal’s energy sector, with the country’s National Energy and Climate Plan (PNEC) targeting 3 GW of batteries and 3.9 GW of pumped hydro by 2030. APREN’s most recent annual review found around 20 MW of installed batteries and 2.8 GW of pumped hydro deployed in Portugal by the end of last year.
Serôdio said that while the strong performance of renewable generation is forecast to continue throughout the rest of 2026, it remains urgent to accelerate both administrative processes and structural investments in order to maintain growth pace and fully integrate the clean energy produced.
She added that strong investor interest remains, with approximately €60 billion in blocked investment intentions waiting to be deployed, but said reducing licensing times to under three years and reforming taxes like the CESE will be crucial unlocking these investments.
“Unblocking these investments is an essential step to meet the PNEC 2030 targets, which require installing an additional 22.2 GW of renewable capacity,” Serôdio said. “Furthermore, to ensure this trajectory remains sustainable and resilient, it is an absolute priority to accelerate investments in the modernization of electricity transmission grids, the introduction of new large-scale storage solutions, and the flexibilization of market rules.”
